stories.title: Public sector strike suspended as unions agree pay deal
stories.summary: Plans for a public sector strike tomorrow have been suspended after trade unions agreed a new draft pay deal with the Government. The proposals will deliver pay increases of 10.75% over two years and nine months in a deal that will run to March 2029. Talks concluded at the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) at around 3.30am. Following the negotiations, the Public Services Committee of the Irish Congress of Trade Unions (ICTU) has recommended that unions suspend strike action and other industrial action, including ongoing work-to-rules, to allow unions to consider the document and arrange ballots. The proposed agreement would run from July 2026 to March 2029, and include the following pay terms: 1 September 2026 - a pay adjustment of 2% or a minimum payment of €1,200 whichever is the greater.

stories.summary: A major policing and security operation is in place in Dublin city centre until Friday, as European leaders meet in the capital for an EU summit. Around 50 European leaders are due to attend meetings of European leaders at the Convention Centre on North Wall Quay on Thursday and Friday. Taoiseach Micheál Martin will also host a dinner for visiting leaders in the National Gallery of Ireland on Thursday evening after the summit. Anyone travelling to or around Dublin city centre is being warned to plan their journeys and expect major and prolonged traffic disruption. But what exactly are the traffic restrictions and how will they affect the public? A security cordon was put in place around the Convention Centre in Dublin, including barriers and no-parking restrictions.

stories.title: Nvidia faces scrutiny over China chip ties, CEO affair
stories.summary: Nvidia shed about $430 billion in market value over two sessions as new reports deepened questions about CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with a Chinese businesswoman alleged to be a spy for Beijing. The controversy escalated on several fronts yesterday as allegations emerged that Huang's relationship with Alice Huang aided at least $7.5 billion in Nvidia chip shipments to China and that US Secretary of State Marco Rubio had previously briefed President Donald Trump on the affair. Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer demanded answers from the administration and tighter curbs on chip exports to China, while the company's independent directors hired outside counsel to investigate. Republican US Senator Kevin Cramer from the Senate Banking Committee called on Huang to step down as CEO. "The potential for extortion is so tremendous that something as sensitive as Nvidia chips, I just think he's got to go," Cramer told Politico last night. The allegations have turned Huang's personal conduct into a broader risk for Nvidia, raising questions about the company's governance and its dependence on the CEO who has led it for more than three decades and built it into the dominant supplier of AI chips.

stories.title: Scullion: The Troubles 'made me more determined to play'
stories.summary: The early 1990s in Ireland. The Troubles were still raging and entering a particularly nasty, late phase. Jack Charlton's Republic of Ireland team were the darlings of the nation. The Fianna Fáil government was still riven by internecine struggles. In the midst of it all, Ulster improbably and abruptly became the dominant province in Gaelic football. Between 1991 and 94, the three Ds - as Tony Scullion called them - won four All-Ireland titles in a row - Down winning the first and last of them, with Donegal and Derry claiming their first-ever titles in between. To outsiders, this splurge came entirely without warning. Between Down's third All-Ireland victory in the '60s in 1968 and their bolt-from-the-blue success in 1991, the Ulster champions had lost in 20 out of 22 All-Ireland semi-final appearances. The only exceptions were Armagh's win over Roscommon in 1977 and Tyrone's defeat of Galway in 1986 (Monaghan did sensationally manage to take Kerry to a replay in 1985). Armagh were hockeyed by Dublin in the '77 final with Jimmy Keaveney running up a record personal score, while Tyrone faded against Kerry in '86 after briefly taking a seven-point lead early in the second half. Were there any clues that a sudden renaissance was in the offing? Down's Ross Carr has previously pointed to Ulster colleges' domination of the Sigerson Cup in the 1980s, with Queen's, UUJ and St Mary's all winning titles. For Scullion, an inductee into the football hall of fame at the Gaelic Writers' Association awards, some inspiration was mined from the Railway Cup, a competition in which Ulster have traditionally excelled, even in the dog days.

stories.title: Get Creative: David Kitt on how to make a classic Irish album # 1
stories.summary: In a new series of Get Creative articles, acclaimed singer-songwriter David Kitt revists the creation of his classic debut album The Big Romance, celebrating its 25th anniversary with a series of concerts and a new version of the original album (including five new tracks) enitled The Big Romance: Kittser's Version. Below, David digs into the writing and recording of The Big Romance's opening track... 'Song From Hope St.(Brooklyn, NY)' is the first song on The Big Romance, and it was also the earliest song of mine that appears on the record. Most of the songs on the record were written around 1999/2000, but this one dates back to the summer of 1998 when I spent the summer in New York on a J2 visa. It was one of the best summers of my life. I was making good money working as a doorman on the upper east side and I got to see Nina Simone, Tony Conrad, La Monte Young, Rodchenko and Rothko retrospectives, listened to Wu Tang walking around Staten Island, dug deep into the world of Steve Reich, read The Brothers Karmazov working on the night shift... I could feel my artistic universe expanding exponentially and 'Song From Hope St.' was a breaking wave moment that seemed to capture all that inspiration and stimulation. Listen: The Album that Inspired Me - David Kitt talks to Dave Fanning The first thing me and my friend Ronan Hand did when we got to New York was head for Williamsburg which we had been tipped off about as a cool area that we might be able to afford to live in and there were some cool bars and record shops there that we needed to check out. It was long before the full wave of gentrification and the cultural mix was much more raw and exciting than you find there these days. We pulled a number from a noticeboard in a record shop about a sublet and gave it a call and half an hour later we were talking face to face with a Puerto Rican filmmaker who was off home to shoot a film and was looking for someone to sublet his place. He liked the cut of us and the deal was done. We couldn't believe our luck. Six weeks later we would be living with a cockroach-nuking builder from Clare in Queens but for those blissful six weeks we lived in a huge loft apartment with a wild expansive view of Manhattan and the most insane record collection and hifi setup including a hammock set up in between two speakers.

stories.title: Traffic restrictions set to ramp up ahead of EU meetings
stories.summary: Traffic restrictions and road closures around Dublin are set to increase significantly today. It comes as delegates arrive for two major EU Presidency meetings in the capital tomorrow and Friday. There will be rolling road closures between Dublin Airport and Casement Aerodrome and the city centre, with the greatest disruption expected on these routes in the afternoon and evening, from 1pm and 11pm. A security cordon is in place around the National Gallery on Merrion Square from 7am this morning. Restrictions around the Convention Centre will also be extended this evening, resulting in the closure of the Samuel Beckett Bridge from 8pm. Traffic and parking restrictions will also be imposed around hotels associated with the meetings in north and south Dublin.

stories.title: Govt must 'pull finger out', publish Climate Action Plan
stories.summary: The Government has been told to "pull the finger out" and publish the Climate Action Plan for 2026. The plan is a roadmap for Ireland meeting its national and EU climate obligations and for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Ireland's Climate Act commits the State to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 51% by 2030, compared with 2018 levels, and to achieving climate neutrality by 2050. At this morning's meeting of the Cabinet, Minister for Climate Darragh O'Brien sought Government approval for the draft of the next update to the plan in advance of the environmental assessment screening process. The plan is expected to be published before the end of the year. However, the Government has been accused by Opposition parties of retreating from climate action.

stories.title: Anthropic eyes $1.4 trillion Wall Street IPO valuation
stories.summary: Anthropic's blockbuster IPO will value the Claude chatbot creator at up to $1.4 trillion, slightly short of some investors' expectations, setting up a key test of Wall Street's faith in the AI boom it helped ignite. The company is kicking off the roadshow for a share sale expected to set a benchmark for the sector, following years of hype that fueled a massive influx of capital into AI companies and sent the US stock market to all-time highs. Anthropic's owners are plowing ahead despite a recent selloff across the tech landscape, as investors question whether the AI boom's returns will justify the massive spending and mounting debt costs in an elevated interest-rate environment. The AI lab and some of its existing shareholders are aiming to raise up to $64.4 billion in the IPO by selling 825 million shares priced between $70 and $78 each. Shares are expected to start trading on the Nasdaq on November 19 under the symbol "ANT." Anthropic will also raise $26 billion via a separate private placement deal with cornerstone investors, including Alphabet's Google, Nvidia - whose CEO is subject to a probe over his affair with an alleged Chinese spy - and Advanced Micro Devices. The IPO is the year's most closely watched since Elon Musk's SpaceX, which raised $75 billion at a nearly $1.75 trillion valuation in June.

stories.title: Wenger to make decision on running for FIFA presidency
stories.summary: Arsene Wenger will make his mind up about whether to stand for the FIFA presidency by the end of this week. The Frenchman, 77, is giving thought to running against incumbent Gianni Infantino, who has lost the confidence of European football's governing body UEFA over a controversial plan to seek private investment in a World Cup company. Sources close to former Arsenal manager Wenger have indicated he will make a final decision on whether to stand this week, with the deadline for candidates to declare falling next Wednesday, 18 November. UEFA stated in August it would work to identify a credible candidate to stand against Infantino, and Wenger would certainly fit the bill and is being encouraged to stand by UEFA. One senior figure in European football believes Wenger is the only person who could beat Infantino and put football first. For months UEFA has sought to identify someone with sufficient global appeal to run against Infantino, but has been at pains to ensure there was no sense of a candidate who was too European being imposed on the world game. Wenger is European but has been FIFA's chief of global football development since November 2019 and is a respected figure worldwide having coached in Japan as well as with huge success in the Premier League. He is also thought to command strong respect in Africa thanks to his development work within FIFA.

stories.title: Review: Saoirse Ronan's directorial debut Paper Plane
stories.summary: Having already been nominated for best acting Oscars on no less than four occasions, what are the chances of Saoirse Ronan finally clinching a gold statuette from the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences with her directorial debut? The actress's 15-minute short, Paper Plane, which she also wrote, recently won Best Narrative Short at the Austin Film Festival, securing the film’s eligibility for Oscar consideration, and it is now set to make its Irish premiere this Friday at the Cork International Film Festival. Described by Ronan, who, at 32, is already an industry veteran, as "a love letter to a younger version of myself, and a younger version of my mother," it is a moving and thought-provoking portrait of a mother and daughter relationship in freefall. Martha Malone (Mayfair Witches, Moonhaven) plays Fay, a defiant young girl who stages a silent protest, communicating only with notes written on paper planes and refusing to return home until her disruptive father leaves the house. She takes up residence under a nearby tree opposite her family home with only her dog for company and a war of wills commences between herself and her mother, played with beautifully judged restraint by KIN and Herself actress Clare Dunne. Almost totally devoid of dialogue, the rustle of suburban trees and the boom of distant traffic (and great use of an Aretha Franklin song) are often the only sound, adding to the film’s subtlety and ambiguity. This is an elegantly shot - the nighttime scenes are deeply evocative - and emotionally-charged two-hander with a singularly determined performance from Malone as the headstrong Fay.

stories.title: Cork teenager on life with a stoma bag
stories.summary: Diagnosed with Crohn's, a chronic inflammatory bowel disease that affects the gastrointestinal tract, when she was just 11, Lydia O'Connell has endured years of symptoms and complications. What began as swelling and pain around her mouth quickly turned into a year-long battle to get a correct diagnosis. This was made all the more difficult by the COVID-19 pandemic. "I was 11, and it was the pandemic, so I was already trying to get used to social distancing and stuff like that," explains the Leaving Cert student. According to the HSE, Crohn's disease is a lifelong condition that leads to parts of the digestive system becoming inflamed, and can often begin in childhood and early adulthood. As well as battling severe fatigue and sharp pains, O'Connell suffered side effects from her medication, including hair loss and nausea. Medication failure also led to arthritis and psoriasis. "It was the week of my [confirmation], and I broke out all over my hands and all over my scalp, all over my legs, all over my stomach," she says of her experience with psoriasis, an autoimmune condition that causes skin cells to multiply too quickly.

stories.title: US judge rejects BBC bid to dismiss Trump defamation case
stories.summary: A federal judge has allowed US President Donald Trump's multi-billion dollar defamation suit against the BBC to proceed, rejecting a bid by the British broadcaster to dismiss the case. Mr Trump has accused the BBC of deceptively editing a documentary to make it seem as if he was inciting violence when he told supporters to march on the US Capitol on 6 January, 2021. He has sought at least $5 billion (€4.44bn) each for one claim of defamation and a separate claim under a Florida consumer protection law. US District Judge Jeffrey Kuntz rejected the BBC's bid to dismiss the defamation suit. But the judge also dismissed the Florida protection law claim. "Whether President Trump can prove these claims and establish he sustained damages at summary judgment or trial is left for another day," Judge Kuntz wrote in a 40-page ruling.

stories.title: Wicklow Gaol to reopen to public this month
stories.summary: The historic Wicklow Gaol is due to reopen its doors this month after renovations and the appointment of a new operator following its closure last September. Wicklow County Council has announced that a new operator has been appointed to run the popular tourist attraction in Wicklow town after a public procurement process. "With updated exhibits, curated storytelling and seasonal events in development, the newly managed Gaol is positioned to reinforce its status as a premier tourist attraction and an economic driver for the region," the council said in a statement. Exhibitions at Wicklow Gaol cover the history of the 1798 Rebellion, the Famine, the Irish War of Independence and Civil War. The grounds of the gaol will open first, with a Christmas market starting on 21 November and running each weekend until 20 December. Tours of the gaol itself will begin from 27 November and run seven days a week.

stories.title: Sport integrity chief explains Man City punishment delay
stories.summary: Fans must be patient for the appeal outcome in the Manchester City case because it "cannot leave room for doubt", a sport integrity chief has said. The club were found guilty by an independent commission of breaking Premier League financial rules over a nine-season period, with the judgement made public on 29 September. The commission found City clearly intended to breach the rules by inflating revenues or reducing costs by more than £900million through a series of "sham" arrangements in order to avoid breaking league and UEFA financial regulations. The club have appealed against the commission's decision, meaning the English top-flight season continues without a final outcome or knowledge of what sanctions – if any – the club may face. That has led some observers to call into question the integrity of what unfolds on the pitch across the rest of the season, but Emanuel Macedo de Medeiros, the co-founder and global chief executive of Sport Integrity Global Alliance (SIGA), insisted the overriding priority must be to ensure justice is served. "I understand the fans’ frustration, and I understand also the fans’ anguish, especially those who follow and support Manchester City," he said.

stories.title: Focal Factor - the comedy quiz show giving Gaeilge a go
stories.summary: Focal Factor Live! is an irreverent comedy panel show in English and Irish, aimed at the people who have 'locked away' the 14 years of school Irish in their brains In this bilingual quiz, two teams battle it out, playing with the Irish language in an unruly way, hosted by Bean an Tí, Sinéad Dolan with Cigire, Rossa Ó Snodaigh (of Irish folk legends Kílá) on hand to help their attempts answering in Irish, with team captains, comedians John Colleary and Sharon Mannion and guests. "I ask the questions in English and the contestants answer in whatever Irish they can" said creator and quizmaster, Sinéad Dolan. "The focus is on re-igniting and using the Irish that's already in your head, by giving you a context to use it". And what better way to do it, than through humour? "People think they don't have it or can't speak it," says Sinéad, "but they just need a chance to use it". "It's totally bilingual, everything is translated on the fly, so non-Irish speakers, learners, returners and Gaeilgeoirí all enjoy it" added Rossa Ó Snodaigh. "I always loved the fact that we have our own secret language, that most of us only use abroad, when we're talking about someone behind their back", laughed Sinéad, "but I want us not to be afraid to use it in Ireland. John, Sharon and I have school Irish, so we are perfect examples of how it's okay to just give Gaeilge a go".

stories.title: Taking stock: The rise of brazen shoplifting and fight to stop it
stories.summary: The lady who comes into the Circle K shop is casually, but tidily, dressed. Probably in her mid-20s with her brown hair tied up in a bun and smart phone in her back pocket, she looks like a normal customer. She has a backpack strapped on her front and a plastic shopping bag in her hand. She approaches a fridge and takes out one can of energy drink and puts it into her backpack. Then another, and another. Altogether, her hand goes in and out of the fridge 18 times as her backpack gets heavier and heavier. She then moves to other parts of the shop, grabbing bundles of chocolate and other items. She fills her plastic shopping bag, too, and then walks out. She has just stolen, perhaps, €200 worth of products. She is clearly identifiable beneath visible CCTV cameras but doesn't appear to care. "This individual has made no attempt to disguise themselves in any way, shape or form, is not wearing a mask, but has come in believing that there's no repercussions effectively for carrying out this activity," said Mark Gannon, Circle K Ireland's Senior Manager for Health Safety and Environment. The woman is part of what Circle K and other retailers say is a growing trend of brazen shoplifting.

stories.title: Mitchell reveals he suffered heart attack against Cats
stories.summary: Offaly hurler Charlie Mitchell has revealed he suffered a heart attack during this year's Leinster SHC clash with Kilkenny, and says there is no timeline in place for a return to play. Mitchell, who played all 70 minutes of the 0-24 to 1-21 draw last May and scored a point, was assessed by the Offaly medical team and taken to Midlands Regional Hospital in Tullamore after the full-time whistle. A decision was made to transfer the 22-year-old to St James' Hospital in Dublin and he underwent what the county are describing as a procedure. Speaking to TG4 at the weekend, the Kilcormac-Killoughey forward also revealed that he suffered a cardiac arrest in hospital after the game. "During the Kilkenny game I had a heart attack during the game and went into hospital," he said. "I had a cardiac arrest after in the hospital and thank God I was in great hands in the hospital. I was lucky that the pitch is so close to the hospital in Tullamore and I was able to get over there quickly and all that, and they looked after me.

stories.title: World leaders take stage at COP31 but big names missing
stories.summary: World leaders will take the stage at COP31 in Turkey but some prominent names are missing from this year's annual UN climate summit even as global warming intensifies. The two-week conference kicked off earlier this week in the Mediterranean resort city of Antalya, with governments under pressure to tackle the climate crisis after a year of heatwaves in Europe, deadly floods in Nepal and major wildfires in Indonesia. Dozens of leaders will speak during the "high-level segment" taking place today and tomorrow, including Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Iran's Masoud Pezeshkian. However, observers have pointed to the absence of some big names, with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham the only leader from a G7 country scheduled to address the summit. While European Union chief Ursula von der Leyen is coming to Antalya, French President Emmanuel Macron, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni are skipping the event. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Japanese counterpart Sanae Takaichi are also absent from the most recent list.

stories.title: Michael O'Sullivan Trophy to honour leading jump jockey
stories.summary: Ireland's champion claiming professional jump jockey will be presented with the Michael O’Sullivan Trophy from this season. The championship has been permanently renamed to commemorate the rider who died in February of last year after suffering a fall at Thurles 10 days earlier. O’Sullivan captured the 2022/2023 Irish National Hunt Champion Claiming Professional crown after riding 32 winners during a remarkable breakthrough season and his family have expressed their pride that the title is now being named in his honour. "We are deeply touched that Michael’s memory will be carried forward through the presentation of the Michael O’Sullivan Trophy to the champion claiming professional at the culmination of each jump season," the O’Sullivan family said in a statement. "Michael poured his heart into his riding and loved the racing community. To have his name permanently attached to the title he was so proud to win is a beautiful and fitting tribute to his legacy." O’Sullivan enjoyed multiple Grade One victories aboard Barry Connell’s Marine Nationale, most notably steering him to success in the Supreme Novices’ Hurdle at the 2023 Cheltenham Festival, where he also went on to land the Fred Winter Juvenile Handicap Hurdle on Jazzy Matty for Gordon Elliott.

stories.title: Charities processed 1m bags of unusable clothes last year
stories.summary: Charity shops have to process nearly a fifth of the country's waste clothing, which comes from textile donations that are not fit for sale, the group representing the sector has said. Charity Retail Ireland said its 43 members that operate retail shops to raise funds for their causes now process about 18% of Ireland's waste textiles, which it said is "a resource-intensive process that detracts efforts from the causes charitable organisations were established to support". The group said that "at a national level, unwanted clothing and textile waste, (which is referred to as post-consumer textiles) is a growing area of concern". It noted that Ireland generates almost double the European average of post-consumer textiles per head (31kg vs 16kg), according to the Natex 2.0 report commissioned by the Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment. It said its member charities processed over 11 tonnes of unsold textiles in 2025, "equivalent to over one million bin bags of clothing which are not fit for sale". Meanwhile, the Charity Retail Ireland Impact Report for 2025 found that €73 million was generated in sales by 407 charity shops around Ireland last year.

stories.title: McCabe an unused substitute as Chelsea held by Hacken
stories.summary: Republic of Ireland international Katie McCabe was an unused substitute as Chelsea were held to a goalless draw against Hacken in their Women's Champions League clash. A frustrating first half for the Blues in Gothenburg saw them have two goals disallowed while Hacken goalkeeper Jennifer Falk made some important stops throughout the contest. The Blues remain unbeaten in the Champions League, but ultimately slipped to their second draw from four outings. McCabe, who was today nominated for a sixth time for the FAI Senior Women’s International Player of the Year and is also in the running for Goal of the Year, watched the 90 minutes unfold from the bench. The Dubliner has not featured in their last three European outings, missing the draw with Lyon through illness and failing to see game time against both Hacken and Roma. Wieke Kaptein headed home for Chelsea in the opening minutes, but the goal was chalked off when Lexi Potter was ruled to have fouled goalkeeper Falk.

stories.title: Parrott in running for trio of FAI awards
stories.summary: Troy Parrott is in the running for the FAI Young and Senior Men's International Player of the Year award, as well as Goal of the Year after his outstanding goalscoring exploits in green. The 24-year-old was instrumental in the Republic of Ireland's bid to reach the summer's World Cup, netting a brace against Portugal last November and backing that up three days later with a hat-trick against Hungary as the Boys in Green secured an unlikely place in the World Cup play-offs. The Dubliner netted against Czechia, but penalty shootout heartache ultimately ended hopes of qualification. The awards take into account performances between June 2025 and May 2026. Parrott is a first-time nominee for the senior award, similar to defender Dara O’Shea, while goalkeeper Caoimhín Kelleher is shortlisted for a second successive year. Parrott’s competition for the Young Player of the Award includes Evan Ferguson – bidding to win the award for a third time – and defender James Abankwah.

stories.title: US charges three 'Iranian operatives' in UK airbase plot
stories.summary: The US Justice Department has announced charges against three men it described as "Iranian operatives", including one already in jail, over their role in an alleged terrorist plot at Britain's RAF Fairford airbase. Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, Mohsen Mohajeri and Mohammad Ali al-Hassani allegedly helped plan and direct the September incident at the base, which has been used by the US military in its operations against Iran. Police were called to the Fairford site in southwest England after a local farmer reported seeing a group of men with several white vans engaged in "suspicious" activity. A US charging document states that Al-Hassani, a 35-year-old Iraqi national, directed unnamed individuals to drive to the base in the vans, some of which contained barrels of fuel. It claims that he earlier paid the group to buy metallic objects that could be used as shrapnel, and to disguise the vehicles as being engaged in fuel delivery services. Al-Saadi, 32, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national already jailed in New York on terrorism charges, allegedly passed coded messages to Al-Hassani and Mohajeri, 48, an Iranian national, to coordinate ahead of the plot.

stories.title: Zelensky welcomes 'changes' in US approach
stories.summary: Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky said he was "happy" with US mediators' change in approach during talks with Russia in Abu Dhabi, set to continue into a second day, but emphasised the need for security guarantees for his country. Representatives from Ukraine and Russia began negotiations in the Emirati capital yesterday, the first since February when discussions reached a stalemate and the US was sidetracked by the Iran war. US envoys, including President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner and businessman Steve Witkoff, are mediating the talks. The first meeting lasted several hours and aimed to make progress towards resolving the war in Ukraine and - according to the US - working on a "new" security framework that includes Europe. Mr Kushner told delegates the United States had "narrowed the gaps" between the warring sides, without providing details, and hoped to move towards a "solution" to Europe's worst conflict since World War II. Mr Zelensky, speaking in Copenhagen yesterday, said the talks were "constructive and quite substantive", adding his team had reported that humanitarian issues and security guarantees were among the topics discussed.

stories.title: Taoiseach favours 'growing football on all-island basis'
stories.summary: Taoiseach Micheál Martin has said he would like to see the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) and the Irish Football Association (IFA) work together to create opportunities to develop football on an all-island basis. He was speaking at Tallaght Stadium ahead of an event celebrating the life and impact of Oscar Traynor, a former Fianna Fáil TD and minister who later served as president of the FAI. Unlike GAA or rugby, football on the island of Ireland has been split between two separate governing bodies since 1921. Asked whether he would be in favour of an all-island international team, the Taoiseach said he favored exploring any initiatives that help develop football across the island. He said he thought the evolution of how soccer developed across the island predated partition. "Soccer was very working class, strongly supported by working class communities," he said.

stories.title: Bohs confirm they will play LOI games at Laya Arena
stories.summary: Bohemians have confirmed they will play a number of their SSE Airtricity Men's Premier Division games at the Laya Arena next season. Bohs will continue to play at Dalymount Park until May of next year before vacating the old ground to facilitate redevelopment works. Work on a new 8,000-seater stadium is due for completion in 2029. The club had previously said the men's team will play at more than one venue while the redevelopment is ongoing. On Tuesday, Bohs revealed that an agreement has been reached with the RDS to host LOI fixtures in Ballsbridge next season. They are still in negotiations to find a second primary home venue "at another League of Ireland stadium". The women's team will play their league matches at Frank Cooke Park, home of Tolka Rovers. The Laya Arena - home to Leinster Rugby - had its full opening in October after a €52m overhaul. "Hosting games at the RDS is a massive positive for the club and a great opportunity for us," said Bohemians president Matt Devaney.
